ABOUT.heading: SLIIQQUE Studio is a Lagos creative studio producing AI commercials, UGC and photography for modern brands.
ABOUT.body: AI is how we produce, not what we sell. We build creative systems, concept, art direction, production, motion and campaign assets, with photorealistic digital humans whose identity holds from the first frame to the last.
stats: Creative services under one studio, run as retainers and content systems.
Complete concept brand worlds built end to end: ÀLÀ, ODÈ and ÀSE.

ala-skin.overview: ÀLÀ is a fictional clinical skincare brand for melanin-rich skin, built by SLIIQQUE as a self-initiated concept project. “Àlà” is Yoruba for clean or pure. The brief we set ourselves: launch a premium skincare brand, led by a 10% niacinamide + 2% zinc serum, for the Lagos woman who already reads ingredient lists and shops The Ordinary, CeraVe or Paula's Choice, without launching a real product.
ala-skin.challenge: Imported clinical brands like The Ordinary and CeraVe are formulated for temperate climates, and local “natural” brands lean on story over evidence. We positioned ÀLÀ between them, clinical warmth, a chemist who also understands Lagos humidity and melanin-rich skin, and held every image to a standard that makes a potential client ask who shot it.
ala-skin.results: A brand concept and strategy, mood board and brand guidelines; a five-product line; 12 product stills, 3 lifestyle images and 6 ad creatives; 4 posters, 14 mockups, two vertical-video storyboards and a landing page. Every image was written as a production brief, lens, light, film stock, composition, grade.
ala-skin.conclusion: ÀLÀ's own line is that skincare should be proven, not promised, and we held the art direction to the same standard: the art direction is the deliverable, the images are its proof. ÀLÀ is concept work with no sales or audience figures, and we present it as exactly that.

ode.overview: ODÈ is a fictional men’s grooming brand rooted in West African heritage, Yoruba for “hunter”, with the line “Discipline. Inherited.” We built it as a self-initiated concept project to show range beyond a single aesthetic lane.
ode.challenge: Prove that photorealistic AI people can stay recognisably the same person from shot to shot. We wrote the production system before generating a frame: a verbatim identity lock pasted into every prompt, continuity tracked across nine domains and a 15-point quality checklist.
ode.results: Brand strategy and a 90-day plan; five campaign concepts; six locked digital-human subjects with identity anchors; a prompt library; 25 AI-generated images; and a full production bible for a 60-second commercial, “The Man Before The Morning”, 38 planned shots across 11 scenes, with 11 shot modules specified. The film itself is not yet rendered.
ode.conclusion: The system was built before the images. A single campaign tells one story; five campaigns tell a world. ODÈ is concept work with no commercial metrics, and we present it as exactly that.

ase.overview: ÀSE is a fictional African-origin luxury spirits brand, Yoruba for the power that makes things happen, built as a self-initiated concept project for the man who doesn't announce his arrival. The line centres on a single-origin African whiskey, aged with intention, and a palm wine spirit, reimagined, pale gold and ancestral. Its line: “The liquid is the argument.”
ase.challenge: Luxury spirits is the most technically demanding category in AI product photography: glass refraction, liquid caustics, smoke and amber light, with the whiskey's dark amber and the palm spirit's pale gold staying continuous bottle to bottle. The brand also had to sit between imported prestige labels and local labels that carry culture without perceived quality, for affluent professionals across Lagos, Accra, London and Johannesburg who can afford anything but choose carefully.
ase.results: A brand system with strategy and research across eight competitors; 33 prompt templates; 25 AI-generated images (14 product stills, 8 lifestyle and 3 ad creatives); three video storyboards, a poster set, 18 mockup specs and a website.
ase.conclusion: ÀSE never explains itself; it states, pauses and moves on, and the images were held to the same restraint. Prompt engineering is brand engineering. ÀSE is concept work with no sales or distribution, and we present it as exactly that.

BLOGS: Why every digital human needs a character lock.
AI fashion imagery: photorealistic models wearing your clothes.

groups: A digital human is only useful to a brand if the audience meets the same person every time. Left alone, image models drift between generations: the jaw softens, the skin tone shifts, a scar moves. A campaign of ten images quietly becomes ten different people.
A character lock is how we stop that. It is a written, permanent description of the person, reused word for word in every prompt.
Start with a profile, not a prompt

Before anything is generated, we study reference images and write an identity profile: face shape, skin and undertone, hair, brows, eyes, nose, lips, ears, age and proportions. The profile is written once and never paraphrased.

In our ODÈ concept work, each of six digital-human subjects has an identity anchor, a fixed description pasted into every prompt for that person. Paraphrasing is where drift begins, so nothing is reworded.

One rule sits above the rest: do not change, beautify, reshape or replace the face. When a result drifts, we re-attach the reference and treat the face as a locked asset instead of rewording the prompt.
Identity lock is what makes AI UGC and digital-human spokespeople viable for brands: the same person across every ad, cut and format. It is the part of the process we are least willing to rush.
Our digital-human work to date is concept work. We use it to prove the method, not to imply client results.
Plan the sequence before making motion

Our storyboard step starts with a single reference image and ends with a single image: a 3×3 grid of nine equal panels, no text. It lets us judge a whole sequence at a glance before any animation is made.
The grid follows a nine-beat story map: setup, setup, rising, rising, turning, turning, climax, resolution, and a closing image that echoes the first panel.
Across all nine panels the face, age, skin tone, body, hair and clothing stay identical, and so do the location and lighting direction. Nothing unrelated is allowed into the frame.

Each panel uses a different camera position (wide establishing, medium, close-up, extreme close-up, point of view, over the shoulder, top-down, low angle and Dutch tilt) so the sequence has rhythm instead of nine versions of one shot.
If a face drifts, we re-attach the reference and treat it as a locked asset, or add a closer face crop as a second reference. If detail is low, we upscale the sheet or generate it in two passes.

Consistency breaks when every stage tries to improve the picture. So we split the job: upscaling makes the source bigger and cleaner, and grading makes the colour decisions, and each happens exactly once.

Our upscale target is a clean, high-resolution frame, flat and neutral with no grade applied. The rule is simple: never hallucinate detail. Sharp without being oversharpened, clean without being plastic, detailed without being noisy.

Every frame is compared with the one beside it for sharpness, noise, brightness, colour temperature and face. A frame that fails is reprocessed with identical settings. Batch consistency outranks per-image perfection.
Colour is corrected and matched across the whole set, with skin and brand colours protected and every adjustment logged. Skin and identity outrank the look, and the sequence outranks the frame.
A viewer should be unable to point at any single frame and say ‘this one was graded harder’. That is the real test of a graded sequence.
A hard limit, turned into a method
The animation tool we use renders a maximum of ten seconds per block. Instead of fighting that, we plan for it: every scene is broken into ten-second animation blocks before anything is rendered.
Each block gets its own specification, the avatar or subject reference, expression, pose, gaze and camera movement, so identity and intent are fixed before the render.
The tool does not handle transitions, so blocks are joined as editor cuts in post. Planning scenes in multiples of ten seconds keeps the timing clean.
Vertical cuts for short-form platforms are built in ten-second multiples too, so a long piece and its cutdowns come from the same blocks.
The limit forces a storyboard-first habit that improves the work. The same discipline applies to AI commercials, UGC and any animated sequence we build.
Why we do not sell single assets

A single image or a single video is easy to commission and hard to use. A brand needs a system: concept, art direction, identity, production, motion and campaign assets that all follow the same rules.
Our creative services run as monthly retainers and content systems, so the identity lock, grade and prompt system built once keeps paying off in every asset that follows.

Our monthly retainers start at ₦150,000 (US$280) for four vertical videos and eight high-resolution stills, move to ₦350,000 (US$650) for eight videos, sixteen stills and a locked digital human, and reach ₦750,000 (US$1,400) for a monthly commercial plus always-on content.

For one-off work we quote a fixed scope: an AI commercial from ₦350,000 (US$650), a product photo pack at ₦75,000 (US$140), a custom digital human at ₦150,000 (US$280), or a 21-day brand launch campaign at ₦900,000 (US$1,700). A 50% deposit starts the work and 50% is due on delivery.
Every engagement begins with one question: how should this brand look, feel and communicate? The system follows from the answer.

AI fashion imagery is photorealistic imagery of AI-generated models wearing a brand’s clothes. It is produced from photos of the real garments, without a studio, a model booking or a wardrobe shoot, and it works for lookbooks, campaign visuals and e-commerce pages.

The garment is the product, so it is never redesigned. SLIIQQUE writes a permanent profile of each piece covering colour, cut, fabric, trim and any print or detail that must not drift, then uses it in every image.
The model is an identity-locked digital human, described once and reused word for word, so the same person wears the whole collection across every image. A custom model is exclusive to the client.

One garment can be shown in different poses, settings and lighting while the colour and construction stay the same. Stills are upscaled without invented detail and graded once as a set so the collection looks like one shoot.

AI fashion imagery suits lookbooks, product pages, ads and social content. Where exact fit or fabric behaviour must be documented, keep real garment photography alongside it. SLIIQQUE will say when a traditional shoot is the better choice.
Models are synthetic: no fabricated customer reviews, no deepfakes of public figures, and no likeness of a real person without their written consent.

ABOUT_PAGE.faq_intro: Straight answers on scope, payment and ownership.
faq: Eight creative services: AI commercials, AI UGC, AI photography, AI fashion imagery, brand launches, product cinematography, visual campaigns and digital humans.
No. We do not offer logo design. Our work starts from your existing brand, or from a creative direction agreed with you in writing.

Mostly no. Ongoing work runs as monthly retainers from ₦150,000 (US$280). One-off projects are fixed-scope: an AI commercial from ₦350,000 (US$650), a product photo pack at ₦75,000 (US$140), a custom digital human at ₦150,000 (US$280) and a brand launch campaign at ₦900,000 (US$1,700).

One-off projects take a 50% deposit to start and 50% on delivery of the final files. Retainers are billed monthly in advance. Nigerian clients pay in naira and international clients in US dollars, by bank transfer. Deposits are non-refundable; if you cancel mid-project you pay for the work done to date.
On full payment, the final deliverables created for you are assigned to you. We keep our pre-existing tools, models and workflows, and license them to you as they appear inside your deliverables.

Extra videos are ₦40,000 (US$75) each, extra stills ₦5,000 (US$10) and extra revision rounds ₦15,000 (US$30). Paid-ad licensing is +30% of the monthly fee where it is not already included, and rush delivery is +50%. Prices exclude taxes.
do you work with international clients?

Yes. We are based in Lagos and work with clients worldwide. International clients are quoted and invoiced in US dollars from our USD price list, paid by international bank transfer. Our Terms & Conditions and Studio Policies set out revisions, delivery, usage rights and cancellation.
Changes are agreed in writing as a change order that states the impact on timeline and budget. After delivery, we fix anything that does not match the agreed scope for 30 days at no cost.
